subject: Pathology
summary: Diffuse Alveolar Damage (DAD) is the histologic hallmark of ARDS, showing widespread injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier with hyaline membranes and edema. It leads to severe hypoxemia and stiff lungs that require ventilatory support.

sections.p: DAD is the microscopic pattern of injury seen in acute respiratory distress syndrome, defined by diffuse alveolar wall damage, hyaline membranes, edema, and inflammation. Diagnosis requires clinical ARDS criteria plus lung biopsy or autopsy showing these features.
b: Clinical ARDS criteria (Berlin): acute onset, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg, bilateral infiltrates, no cardiac cause
Histology: hyaline membranes, interstitial edema, type II pneumocyte hyperplasia

t.b: Diffuse ground‑glass opacities support ARDS; focal infiltrates suggest pneumonia
Low ratio confirms ARDS severity; normal ratio argues against DAD
Hyaline membranes and edema confirm DAD; absence suggests other pathology

sections.p: Berlin criteria stage ARDS as mild (200‑300), moderate (100‑200), or severe (<100) based on PaO2/FiO2 with PEEP ≥5 cmH2O. Histologically, DAD progresses from exudative (0‑7 days) to proliferative (7‑21 days) to fibrotic (>21 days).
b: Proliferative: type II cell hyperplasia, fibroblast infiltration

sections.p: Identify the inciting insult; most common are sepsis, aspiration, severe pneumonia, and trauma. In low‑resource settings add malaria, severe dengue, TB, HIV‑related opportunistic infections, and herbal toxin exposure.
b: Disseminated TB or PCP in HIV

t.b: Recent infection, trauma, or toxin points to DAD cause; no trigger suggests alternative diagnosis

sections.p: Patients develop rapid onset dyspnea, tachypnea, and hypoxemia refractory to oxygen, often with diffuse crackles. The chest is usually “wet” but the heart sounds are normal, distinguishing it from cardiogenic edema.
Use bedside tools first; advanced tests when available. When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and basic imaging.

t.b: Low saturation confirms severe gas exchange defect
Normal/low BNP favors DAD; high BNP suggests cardiac cause

sections.p: Uncontrolled hypoxemia, refractory hypercapnia, and rapid progression to fibrosis are life‑threatening. Secondary infections and barotrauma from ventilation are common complications.
Treat the underlying cause, then provide lung‑protective ventilation and supportive care. Avoid high tidal volumes and liberal fluids.
b: Low tidal volume (6 mL/kg predicted body weight)

t.b: Broad‑spectrum coverage started; de‑escalate when cultures return
Low‑dose steroids may improve outcomes; avoid if active infection
Short‑term paralysis improves oxygenation; monitor for weakness

sections.p: After recovery, assess lung function, monitor for fibrosis, and vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus. Educate on early treatment of infections to prevent recurrence.
Conditions that also cause diffuse infiltrates and hypoxemia but have different pathophysiology.
Certain labs may appear normal despite severe DAD, leading to delayed treatment.
b: BNP may be low even with severe hypoxemia
Chest X‑ray can be deceptively normal early
Lactate may be normal if sepsis is controlled

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe dyspnea with oxygen saturation <80% despite supplemental O2
New onset hypotension or cardiac arrest
